name: Zaffre
lede: Zaffre is the name of an impure cobalt oxide that glassmakers and smalt-makers fused with sand and potash; as a color word it names a raw material, and on screens it is a deep, saturated blue.

sections.title: What zaffre was
sections.body:
Zaffre was a precursor to smalt, the cobalt-blue glass pigment: an impure cobalt oxide mixed with silica and potash and fused (Tingry, 1804) [1]. It was also written saffer, saffre and zaffera [1][2]. Cobalt ore was roasted to an oxide, mixed with quartz sand and sold under these names to glassmakers [2].

The main historical source of the cobalt was the mineral skutterudite, named for Skutterud in Norway and also called smaltite for its use in making smalt, and Saxony supplied the ore for centuries [2]. Smalt itself belongs to the family of cobalt blues, of which [[cobalt]] and [[cobalt-blue]] are the modern members.

sections.title: Books disagree on what it was
sections.body: Heaton (1928) lists saffer as an obsolete word for an impure smalt, which makes zaffre a poor version of the finished pigment [3]. The compendium instead calls it the precursor from which smalt was made [1]. Merrifield (1849) goes further: the Venetian *smalto di Flandra* was zaffre and very close to what is now called smalt, and he separates two pigments both named *azur à poudrer*, the first being a zaffre [1][4]. The compendium adds that fifteenth-century mentions of smalto and smaltino probably did not mean smalt at all [1].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
The swatch is a saturated deep blue (lightness 21, chroma 92, hue 304), listed in ISCC-NBS 1955 as block 179 under the name Zaffre Blue [5]. The library gives Maerz and Paul's first record as about 1554 [5]. Its nearest plain name is [[royal]], and it reads as a cousin of [[indigo]] [5].

The books we hold describe zaffre by function, as a raw material, not by how it looked, so the screen color follows naming convention more than any measured pigment [1][5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The archive finds the swatch in one of 23,781 paintings, and a close look inside paintings finds it in two; it is rarer than 82 per cent of the named colors [6]. In printed English, the word as an adjective, which is the color sense, peaks in the 1860s [7]. All senses of the word, mainly the glassmakers' material, peak earlier, around 1810 [7].
